result.summary: Two short fragments reflect on death. All people reach an end that brings rest from labor, and though the body dies, a shadow of life, which comes from the gods, lives on and in dreams reveals coming joy or sorrow.

scenes.title: Reflection on death and the soul
scenes.summary: The poet says all come to a restful end, and that the soul's image survives the body and speaks in dreams.

notable_quotes.reason: A striking early Greek statement of the soul as a divine shadow that foretells the future in dreams.

analysis.text: The fragments treat death as a release from toil while affirming a divine part of a person that survives the body.
The passage reflects early Greek ideas about the soul, thought to be active in sleep and to give prophetic dreams. Such ideas appear in Pindar's dirges (threnoi).

fun_facts.text: Pindar's lines survive only as quotations in later writers, such as Plutarch, which is why they are called fragments.

language_notes.text: "By happy lot" means by good fortune or fate; "giveth them rest from toils" is archaic third-person -eth verb form, meaning the end brings relief from labors.
"A shadow of life" translates Greek aiōn eidōlon, an image of life: the soul as a phantom-like double of the person.
"Discovereth" means reveals or uncovers; "the judgment that draweth nigh" is the decision of fate approaching, whether bringing grief or joy.

context_notes.text: Pindar here voices an early Greek view that the soul, being divine in origin, is active in dreams while the waking body is busy, a belief tied to prophetic dreaming.

literary_notes.text: The soul is called a "shadow of life," suggesting it is a faint, insubstantial image of the living person that outlasts the body.
The soul sleeps while the limbs are active and wakes in sleep to speak, reversing the usual relation of waking and sleeping.
